docs.title: LLM Abstraction
docs.text: Every LLM call in the system goes through a single one-method interface, returns structured JSON, and never crashes the caller. This page explains that interface, how a provider is selected, the difference between the Azure and mock providers, the full prompt catalog across all three subsystems, and how traces and cost are recorded.

docs.title: The one-method interface
docs.text:
The contract is app/llm/contracts.py, a Protocol with exactly one method:

complete_json(prompt_name, prompt_version, system_prompt, user_payload: dict, response_schema: dict) -> LLMResult

There is no separate complete or chat — everything is structured JSON. The LLMResult (app/schemas/llm.py) carries output_json, provider, model, token_usage, latency_ms, raw_text, and error_message. A companion LLMTraceDraft is persisted to the llm_traces table for every call.

LLM failures never crash the pipeline

On any error — content filter, length truncation, non-JSON output, or a transport failure — the provider returns an LLMResult with error_message set and output_json empty ({}). Callers check the result; they never catch an exception from the provider. This is why every LLM-using step has a deterministic fallback path.

docs.title: Provider selection
docs.text: app/infra.py build_llm_provider() returns an AzureOpenAIProvider when LLM_PROVIDER == azure_openai, otherwise a MockLLMProvider. The CLI has its own _build_llm_provider() that additionally wires a DB session factory so cost-ledger rows can be written from CLI runs.

docs.title: AzureOpenAIProvider
docs.text: app/llm/azure_openai_provider.py lazily constructs openai.AzureOpenAI(azure_endpoint, api_key, api_version="2024-08-01-preview"). The model is AZURE_OPENAI_MODEL (the deployment name, default gpt-4o). It requests response_format={"type": "json_object"} and sets max_completion_tokens to 4096 for the heavy prompts (impact_analysis, competitor_query, maintenance_copilot, final_classifier) and 1024 otherwise. It never raises: content-filter and length-truncation cases become error_message, non-JSON output is wrapped as {"raw_text": ...}. Each call writes an LLMCostLedger row via _write_cost_ledger().

docs.title: MockLLMProvider
docs.text: app/llm/mock_provider.py (PROVIDER="mock", MODEL="mock-v1") is deterministic and does no network I/O. Its _route() dispatches on prompt_name substrings to a canned response for every prompt in the catalog, with fixed token_usage of {prompt: 100, completion: 50, total: 150}. This is what powers the offline test suite (tests run with no keys).

docs.title: The prompt catalog
docs.text: Every prompt used anywhere in the system, grouped by subsystem. All go through complete_json and are recorded as LLMTrace rows.

docs.title: Layer 1 — analysis (max_completion_tokens 1024)
docs.text: Prompt Version Analyzer Purpose website_semantic_diff v1 Website meaningful positioning shift vs noise careers_role_normalizer v1 Careers classify job title → function careers_pattern_interpreter v1 Careers hiring surge / geo expansion → signal news_relevance_resolver v1 News is a borderline article about this competitor news_event_extractor v1 News extract business event + signal_type blog_social_post_interpreter v1 BlogSocial interpret a post → signal

docs.title: Layer 2 — intelligence pipeline
docs.text: Prompt Version Step Purpose signal_normalizer v1 Normalization (4) subject-action-object, normalize entities, claim status event_merge_judge v1 Clustering (8) same real-world event? (conservative) final_classifier v1 Classification (9) one of 10 categories impact_analysis v2 Impact (11) grounded GCP business impact (headline, so_what, threat level) profile_narrative v1 Profile narrative (14) 3–4 sentence executive narrative competitor_query v2 out-of-pipeline NL Q&A over profiles + changes

docs.title: Feedback governance & ops
docs.text:
Prompt Version Where Purpose weight_adjustment v1 legacy feedback scoring-weight deltas from a verdict policy_consolidation v1 POST /admin/policy-health/{id}/consolidate merge / retire / convert policy rules maintenance_copilot v1 POST /admin/observability/copilot ops assistant + action suggestions nl_command v1 POST /admin/feedback/nl-command parse free-text into a governance action

The governance core is deterministic

Feature extraction, pattern mining, and proposal generation use no LLM. The only LLM touch-points in the feedback subsystem are the legacy weight_adjustment call, policy_consolidation, and eval runs that exercise LLM agents. See Feedback & Learning Governance.

The impact_analysis v2 system prompt hardcodes GCP identity, brand/category/market lists, 15 grounding rules, and an exact output-key contract.

docs.title: Traces and cost
docs.text: Every call produces an LLMTrace (provider, model, prompt name/version, input hash, output, token usage, latency, error). The AzureOpenAIProvider additionally writes an LLMCostLedger row, priced from the active LLMPriceCatalog (seeded at startup: input $0.005/1k, output $0.015/1k, cached $0.0025/1k; fallback 0.005/0.015). Costs then roll up through the telemetry hierarchy. See Observability & Telemetry.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Configuration & Environment
  • Observability & Telemetry

docs.title: Observability & Telemetry
docs.text: Every agent step in the system is observed, timed, and costed. This telemetry model is what powers the observability screens in the admin panel — the pipeline board, live run view, cost explorer, and agent-load charts. This page explains the observe_agent() context manager, the telemetry hierarchy, how cost rolls up, and the load-bearing stage-key format you must never change.

docs.title: The observe_agent() context manager
docs.text:
observe_agent() (app/observability/telemetry.py) wraps a unit of agent work and writes exactly one AgentRunTelemetry row:

observe_agent(agent_name, agent_type, workflow, stage, db=..., competitor_id=..., source_id=..., input_count=...)

The row starts running and transitions to success or failed on exit, recording timing, duration_ms, and any error. Inside the block, code calls obs.set_output_count() and obs.set_metadata({...}). Run context (which pipeline run and competitor run a span belongs to) flows through ContextVars set by set_run_context(). Layer 1 wraps the adapter and analyzer; Layer 2 wraps three steps — normalization, classification, and impact_assessment.

docs.title: The telemetry hierarchy
docs.text:
Telemetry nests four levels deep. A PipelineRun contains one CompetitorRun per competitor; each competitor run contains many AgentRunTelemetry spans; and each span that made LLM calls has one or more LLMCostLedger rows. CurrentRunState is a single live-progress row updated as the run advances.

flowchart TD
  PR["PipelineRun<br/>spans L1 + L2 + delivery"]
  CR["CompetitorRun<br/>one per competitor"]
  ART["AgentRunTelemetry<br/>one per agent step"]
  LED["LLMCostLedger<br/>one per LLM call"]
  CRS["CurrentRunState<br/>live progress (single row)"]

  PR --> CR
  CR --> ART
  ART --> LED

  LED -. cost roll-up .-> ART
  ART -. roll-up .-> CR
  CR -. roll-up .-> PR

  PR -. drives .-> CRS

docs.title: Cost propagation and pricing
docs.text: record_llm_cost() writes an LLMCostLedger row per LLM call, and _propagate_cost_to_parent() rolls that cost upward: ledger → AgentRunTelemetry → CompetitorRun → PipelineRun. Prices come from the active LLMPriceCatalog (fallback 0.005/0.015 per 1k tokens). The cost explorer and /admin/observability/costs present totals grouped by agent, competitor, run, or source, and every figure is shown in both USD and INR (USD_TO_INR = 85).

docs.title: The pipeline board key format
docs.text:
The pipeline board (GET /admin/observability/pipeline-board) aggregates AgentRunTelemetry two ways: per-stage stats keyed workflow:stage:agent_name, and per-competitor stage_statuses keyed workflow:stage (for example layer2:classification). STAGE_ORDER lists normalization, classification, impact_assessment.

Never change the workflow:stage key format

The panel JavaScript parses these composite keys to render the board and live-run flowchart. Changing the separator, order, or naming of the workflow:stage (or workflow:stage:agent_name) keys silently breaks the observability UI. Treat the format as a frozen contract. See API — Observability.

docs.title: Live run state
docs.text: GET /admin/observability/runs/current returns the CurrentRunState: current stage/agent/competitor, progress percent, elapsed time, sources and signals done/total, accumulated cost, and the list of active agents. The live-run screen polls this alongside the pipeline board to render a flowchart with a LIVE badge.

docs.title: Timeline and Gantt
docs.text:
GET /admin/observability/runs/{id}/timeline returns AgentRunTelemetry ordered by started_at plus a per-competitor summary, which the panel renders as a Gantt-style timeline. p95 latency figures on the agent-load screen are computed in Python from these spans.

Never print real secrets in telemetry

Telemetry and cost rows are safe to expose in the panel, but prompts and payloads can contain sensitive competitor data. Keep secrets out of logs and metadata; .env, data/*.db, and blobs are never committed.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Admin Panel — Observability Screens
  • API — Observability

docs.title: Scoring & Impact
docs.text:
Significance scoring and impact assessment are the two steps that decide how much a detected change matters and what it means for the business. Scoring is fully deterministic and weighted; impact is the pipeline's primary LLM step, grounded in Godrej Consumer Products (GCP). This page explains how the score is composed, how the bands are decided, how weights are tuned, and how impact analysis differs.

Grounded in GCP

Impact analysis treats Godrej Consumer Products (GCP) as the home company and HUL, P&G India, ITC, Marico, Dabur, and Reckitt as competitors. The impact_analysis prompt (v2) hardcodes GCP brand, category, and market lists.

docs.title: The significance scoring model
docs.text:
score_cluster() (app/intelligence/scoring.py) is pure and deterministic. It sums six positive components, subtracts penalties, optionally applies a source-reliability multiplier, and maps the total to a band. The full breakdown is persisted to SignificanceScore.score_breakdown_json.

Component Contribution Competitor tier Tier1 = 20, Tier2 = 12, Tier3 = 6 Category weight Product Launch / Pricing = 18 … Marketing = 8 Source authority official / first_party = 15 … unknown = 0 Corroboration (distinct source types) 1 → 3, 2 → 8, 3+ → 12 Novelty new = 8, update = 3 Confidence up to 10

Penalties: rumored/speculative −15; weak evidence −10 and weak snippet −5; low classification confidence (< 0.5) −10.

flowchart TD
  T["tier<br/>20 / 12 / 6"] --> SUM["Σ weighted score"]
  C["category weight<br/>18 … 8"] --> SUM
  A["source authority<br/>15 … 0"] --> SUM
  CO["corroboration<br/>3 / 8 / 12"] --> SUM
  N["novelty<br/>8 / 3"] --> SUM
  CF["confidence<br/>≤ 10"] --> SUM
  P["− penalties<br/>rumored / weak / low-conf"] --> SUM
  REL["× source reliability<br/>(optional)"] --> SUM
  SUM --> BAND{total}
  BAND -->|≥ 75| HIGH["High"]
  BAND -->|≥ 40| MED["Medium"]
  BAND -->|≥ 15| LOW["Low"]
  BAND -->|< 15| ARCH["Archive"]

docs.title: Dynamic weights
docs.text:
The orchestrator loads exactly one active ScoringWeightProfile per run. load_active_weights() (app/intelligence/scoring_weights.py) merges that profile's weights_json over DEFAULT_WEIGHTS at the top level, so a profile only needs to specify overrides.

There are two paths that adjust weights from feedback:

  • Governance (deterministic) — approving a scoring_weight_change proposal runs _activate_weight_change, which sets category_scores[cat] to a ±10% adjusted value and inserts a new active profile. See Feedback & Learning Governance.
  • Legacy (LLM) — the immediate feedback path calls decide_weight_adjustments_with_llm and apply_llm_weight_adjustments for the over_rated, under_rated, false_positive, and missed verdicts. Deltas are clamped to [-30, 30], validated, and appended to adjustment_log_json.

See How-to: Tune Scoring Weights for the operator workflow.

docs.title: Source reliability multiplier
docs.text: SourceReliabilityService (app/feedback/source_reliability.py) matches a rule by domain (and optionally source type) and returns a reliability_score (default 1.0). adjust_score clamps base × multiplier into [0, 1], and scoring applies it as an optional multiplier before banding.

docs.title: Impact assessment
docs.text: build_impact_assessment() (app/intelligence/impact.py) is the pipeline's primary LLM step and the only one that consumes the cumulative CompetitorProfile plus recent-change history — which makes it trend-aware. It sends a rich payload (evidence excerpts capped at ~2000 characters × 12, the cumulative profile, and trend history) to the impact_analysis prompt (v2) and extracts headline, summary, so_what, recommended_action, watchpoints, follow-ups, assumptions, and unsupported claims, plus an extended_analysis_json with pattern context, competitive threat level (direct / adjacent / monitor), and affected GCP categories and markets. It also appends any admin prompt addendum via agent_feedback.get_prompt_addendum.

docs.title: Fallback impact when the LLM is absent
docs.text: If no LLM provider is available, _fallback_impact produces a deterministic impact record so the pipeline still yields a usable DetectedChange. As always, LLM failures never crash the run — the provider returns an error_message and empty output instead of raising.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• How-to: Tune Scoring Weights
  • Feedback & Learning Governance

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: This page gives you the whole-system mental model for the Competitive Intelligence Aggregator: the three processing layers (scanning, intelligence, delivery), the admin control plane that drives them, the infrastructure abstractions that make the same code run locally or on Azure, and the telemetry that observes everything. Read it first — every other page in this section zooms into one part of the picture drawn here.

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text:
The application is organized as a linear intelligence assembly line with three stages:

  • Layer 1 — Source scanning (app/adapters/, app/analysis/, app/workers/). For each configured Source, a source-type-specific adapter fetches raw data, persists it to blob storage and the database, and an analyzer diffs it against the previous scan and applies a cheap deterministic gate (plus optional LLM) to emit CandidateSignal rows. See Layer 1 — Source Scanning.
  • Layer 2 — Intelligence pipeline (app/intelligence/). A 15-step orchestrator turns raw CandidateSignal rows into deduplicated, classified, scored, and impact-assessed DetectedChange records, plus delivery artifacts and a cumulative CompetitorProfile. See Layer 2 — Intelligence Pipeline.
  • Layer 3 — Delivery (app/delivery/). The DigestAssembler builds the weekly digest from DetectedChange rows with status ready, and EmailDelivery / TeamsDelivery push it out. High-significance changes also trigger an immediate email alert from inside Layer 2.

docs.title: Control plane and admin
docs.text:
Two entry points drive the layers, and both flow through the repositories layer (app/db/repositories.py) into the database — routes and workers never touch the ORM directly:

  • Config loader — app/admin/yaml_loader.py reads a competitor YAML (for example examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml) and inserts Competitor and Source rows.
  • Admin panel + REST API — a single self-contained page at /admin/panel calls seven FastAPI routers under app/admin/ (routes.py, intelligence_routes.py, observability_routes.py, policy_health_routes.py, schedule_routes.py, scan_request_routes.py, news_profile_routes.py).

docs.title: Infrastructure abstractions
docs.text:
Three capabilities are accessed through protocols so the same business code runs unchanged in either environment. The concrete implementation is chosen by app/infra.py based on ENVIRONMENT and the presence of connection strings:

Capability Protocol Local Azure (production) Job queue SourceScanQueue InMemorySourceScanQueue AzureServiceBusSourceScanQueue Blob storage BlobStore LocalBlobStore (local://) AzureBlobStore (azblob://) LLM LLMProvider MockLLMProvider AzureOpenAIProvider

The database follows the same idea: SQLite (WAL mode) locally, Azure SQL in production, both via SQLAlchemy.

flowchart TB
  classDef llm fill:#efe,stroke:#3fb950,color:#111
  classDef obs fill:#eef,stroke:#58a6ff,color:#111

  subgraph CP["Control plane"]
    YAML["Competitor YAML"] --> LOADER["yaml_loader"]
    PANEL["/admin/panel + 7 routers"]
  end

  LOADER --> DB[("Database<br/>SQLite / Azure SQL")]
  PANEL --> DB

  SCHED["Scheduler<br/>get_due_sources"] --> QUEUE["Queue<br/>InMemory / Service Bus"]
  PANEL -. enqueue only .-> QUEUE
  QUEUE --> WORKER["SourceScanWorker<br/>process_job"]

  subgraph L1["Layer 1 — scanning"]
    WORKER --> ADP["Adapters"]
    ADP --> BLOB[("BlobStore")]
    ADP --> ANA["Analyzers + cheap gate"]
    ANA --> CS["CandidateSignal"]
  end

  subgraph L2["Layer 2 — intelligence"]

  ORCH --> DB

docs.title: Runtime modes
docs.text:
This is the single most important operational fact about the system, and it differs from older internal notes:

In server mode nothing consumes the queue

The only scheduler started by the FastAPI server (app/scheduler/__init__.py) is a WeeklyDigestScheduler (Layer 3 email, Mondays 08:00). It does not run source scans or the worker. Admin scan-requests only enqueue jobs. Actual worker execution is CLI-driven (ci-agent worker-once, ci-agent dev-run-once, ci-agent run-pipeline) or, in production, a separate process consuming Azure Service Bus. If jobs "aren't running," this is almost always why.

docs.title: Cross-cutting concerns
docs.text:
• Telemetry — observe_agent() wraps every agent step in one AgentRunTelemetry row; runs roll up into CompetitorRun and PipelineRun. See Observability & Telemetry.
  • Cost ledger — each LLM call writes an LLMCostLedger row, propagated up the telemetry hierarchy. See LLM Abstraction.
  • Repositories — all persistence flows through app/db/repositories.py (roughly 80 functions); the CLI read commands are the only exception.

verify=False is deliberate

All adapter HTTP (and the permissive email SSL context) intentionally disables certificate verification to work behind the corporate proxy. This is a design decision, not a bug — do not "fix" it. See Configuration & Environment.

docs.title: Project layout tour
docs.text:
app/
  main.py          FastAPI entrypoint (7 routers, /admin/panel, startup)
  cli.py           Typer CLI (ci-agent)
  infra.py         build_queue / build_blob_store / build_llm_provider
  core/            config, enums, errors, hashing, time, urls
  db/              base, session, models, repositories
  llm/             contracts, azure_openai_provider, mock_provider
  adapters/        website, news, careers, blog_social, social + registry
  analysis/        website, news, careers, blog_social + orchestrator, cheap_gate, registry
  intelligence/    orchestrator (15 steps) + normalization, clustering, scoring, impact, ...
  delivery/        digest, email, teams
  storage/ queue/ scheduler/ workers/ admin/ feedback/ observability/

Doc drift correction

The real analysis package is app/analysis/ (not app/analyzers/), observability routes live in app/admin/observability_routes.py (not app/api/), and adapters/analyzers are organized as per-type packages (not flat *_adapter.py files). Where older notes disagree, the code wins.
