docs.title: Get Started Overview
docs.text: This is the guided tutorial track for the Competitive Intelligence Aggregator. Follow it in order and you will go from a clean clone to a running system that scans a competitor, produces a scored intelligence report, and learns from your feedback — all on your own machine, offline, with no API keys required.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
By the end of the track you will have:

  • The app installed and the admin panel open in your browser.
  • Godrej competitors and their sources loaded from YAML.
  • A completed Layer 1 scan producing CandidateSignal rows.
  • A completed Layer 2 run turning those signals into scored DetectedChange deliverables.
  • Your first feedback loop — a verdict on a change that flows into the governance proposal queue.

docs.title: The tutorial path
docs.text:
Work through these pages in sequence. Each one builds on the previous.

  1. Installation & Setup — clone, create a virtual environment, install, and reach the admin panel.
  2. Configuration & First Config Load — set the minimum environment and load competitors from YAML.
  3. Your First Scan (Layer 1) — run dev-run-once and read the candidate signals.
  4. From Signals to a Scored Report (Layer 2) — run layer2-dev-run and read a DetectedChange.
  5. Your First Feedback Loop — submit a verdict and find the resulting governance proposal.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Windows 11 (commands are shown for Windows first, with Linux/Mac equivalents).
  • Python 3.11+ on your PATH.
  • git for cloning the repository.

Tip

The tutorials run entirely offline against the deterministic mock LLM provider and mock news fixtures — no Azure OpenAI or search keys are needed. You only need real keys later, for production-grade runs. See Configuration.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Installation & Setup — start here.

docs.title: Configuration & First Config Load
docs.text: In this tutorial you will understand the two configuration layers, set the minimum environment needed for a real LLM run, and load your first set of competitors and sources from a YAML file. When you finish, the database will contain the Godrej competitor set (HUL, P&G India, Marico, Dabur) and their sources, ready to scan.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You completed Installation & Setup — the app is installed, .env exists, and init-db has run.
  • Your virtual environment is active.

docs.title: 1. The two configuration layers
docs.text:
Configuration comes from two places, and it is important to know which wins:

  1. .env (global defaults) — read by pydantic-settings into a Settings singleton (get_settings()), resolved relative to the project root. This sets provider choices, keys, timeouts, and delivery options.
  2. Per-source YAML config blocks (local overrides) — each Source in the competitor YAML carries a free-form config: block stored as config_json. These override .env for that source (for example, a source can pin provider: tavily regardless of the global NEWS_PROVIDER).

Note

Rule of thumb: .env sets the defaults; a source's config: block overrides them for that source only.

docs.title: 2. Minimum .env for a real-LLM run
docs.text:
The tutorials run offline with the mock provider, so you can skip this step for now. When you are ready for a real run against Azure OpenAI and live news, set these keys — using placeholders here; put real values only in your local, gitignored .env:

LLM_PROVIDER=azure_openai
AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT=https://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com
AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY=<AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY>
AZURE_OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4o
NEWS_PROVIDER=tavily
TAVILY_API_KEY=<TAVILY_API_KEY>

Danger

Never paste real secrets into documentation, commits, or the YAML files. Use placeholders like <AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY> and https://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com. Real values belong only in your local .env, which is gitignored.

For the full list of keys, see Configuration & Environment.

docs.title: 3. The competitor YAML shape
docs.text:
Competitors and their sources are defined in YAML under examples/config/. The shipped file examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml defines Tier-1 competitors and their sources. A single competitor looks like this:

competitors:
  - name: Hindustan Unilever Limited
    tier: Tier1
    aliases: [HUL]
    known_domains: [hul.co.in, unilever.com]
    brand_names: [Dove, Lux]
    negative_terms: [Hulu, Hull City]   # disambiguation
    custom_keywords: [premiumisation, D2C]
    sources:
      - name: HUL website scope
        source_type: website_scope       # website_page | website_scope | news_search | careers | blog | social
        url: https://www.hul.co.in/
        frequency: weekly                 # daily | weekly | manual
        config:                           # free-form; OVERRIDES .env for this source
          seed_urls: [https://www.hul.co.in/brands/]
          include_patterns: [/brands/, /news/]
          exclude_patterns: [/privacy, /cookie]
          max_pages_per_scan: 25
      - name: HUL news search
        source_type: news_search
        config: {provider: tavily, query_budget: 12, recency_window_days: 7}

Top-level fields like aliases, known_domains, and brand_names are stored on the Competitor as *_json columns; each source's config: block is stored as Source.config_json.

Tip

A smaller examples/config/sample_competitors.yaml exists as a lightweight test variant if you want to start with fewer sources.

docs.title: 4. Load the config
docs.text:
Load the competitors and sources into the database:

ci-agent load-config examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml
# equivalent: python -m app.cli load-config examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml

The command reports how many competitors and sources it created.

Warning

load-config always inserts — it has no upsert or dedup logic. Running it a second time on the same file creates duplicate competitors and sources. Load each file once, or clean up duplicates afterward. See Add a Competitor & Sources.

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
Confirm the data landed, either from the panel or the CLI:

ci-agent status

Open http://localhost:8000/admin/panel and check the Admin Control screens — you should see the competitors and their sources listed. See Admin Control Plane.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Your First Scan (Layer 1) — run a scan against the sources you just loaded.
  • Configuration & Environment — the exhaustive key-by-key reference.

docs.title: Tutorial — Your First Feedback Loop
docs.text: In this tutorial you will submit an analyst verdict on a DetectedChange and watch it flow into the governance system as a human-review proposal. This is how the system learns: verdicts become deterministic patterns, patterns become proposals, and approved proposals become active policy that gates and tunes future runs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You completed From Signals to a Scored Report (Layer 2) and have at least one DetectedChange.
  • The server is running (uvicorn app.main:app --reload) if you want to use the panel form.

docs.title: 1. Why feedback exists
docs.text: An analyst reviewing a change can say "this is a false positive," "this was over-scored," or "this needs re-analysis." The system captures the verdict and feeds two subsystems at once: a legacy path that applies some effects immediately, and a governance path that deterministically mines the feedback into proposals requiring human approval before anything changes. See Feedback & Learning Governance.

docs.title: 2. Submit a verdict
docs.text:
Pick a DetectedChange ID from the previous tutorial and submit a verdict. Use the panel form or the CLI.

CLIPanel 
ci-agent feedback-submit --change-id <change-id> --verdict false_positive --reason "Not about a competitor" --analyst you@godrejcp.com
# equivalent: python -m app.cli feedback-submit ...

Open the Changes screen, click your change, fill in the feedback form, and choose a verdict.

The allowed verdicts are: correct, false_positive, low_priority, over_rated, under_rated, needs_reanalysis, missed.

docs.title: 3. What happens immediately vs what's proposed
docs.text:
The two subsystems react differently to the same verdict. For false_positive, for example:

  • Legacy path (immediate): if the corresponding flags are on, it archives the change (status archived_fp) and creates a legacy FeedbackSuppressionEntry for the URL and fingerprint.
  • Governance path (proposed): it extracts deterministic features, mines a pattern, and generates a suppression_rule proposal (on every occurrence) — plus an agent_policy_rule proposal once the pattern has been seen at least twice. These are created with status pending_human_review.

Note

The governance path never auto-approves. It only proposes; a human must review and approve. The legacy path is what applies some effects immediately. The two suppression tables (legacy FeedbackSuppressionEntry and governance SuppressionRule) are separate and not unified.

docs.title: 4. Find the proposal
docs.text:
List the pending governance proposals. From the API/panel:

GET /admin/feedback/proposals

Open the Governance screen in the panel to see the queue. Each proposal shows its type (suppression_rule, scoring_weight_change, agent_policy_rule), its risk level, and the change it derived from. See Feedback & Governance Screens.

docs.title: 5. Approve it and observe the effect
docs.text:
Approve the proposal (optionally editing its change_json first). Approval always activates the proposal regardless of its risk level:

  • A suppression_rule becomes an active SuppressionRule.
  • A scoring_weight_change deactivates the current weight profile and inserts a new active ScoringWeightProfile.
  • An agent_policy_rule becomes an active AgentPolicyRule and triggers a recompile of that agent's policy pack.

Re-run Layer 2 and you should see the new policy take effect — for example, a suppressed signal no longer producing a change.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Feedback & Learning Governance — the full governance lifecycle and diagrams.
  • Review & Approve Feedback Proposals — working the review queue as a task.

docs.title: Tutorial — From Signals to a Scored Report (Layer 2)
docs.text: In this tutorial you will run Layer 2 to turn the candidate signals from your first scan into clustered, classified, scored, and impact-assessed DetectedChange deliverables — the intelligence an analyst actually reads. When you finish, you will have a scored report you can inspect from the CLI and the admin panel.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You completed Your First Scan (Layer 1) and have CandidateSignal rows with status candidate.
  • Your virtual environment is active.

Note

If your first scan produced only a baseline (zero signals), run ci-agent dev-run-once a second time so there are change-driven signals for Layer 2 to process.

docs.title: 1. What Layer 2 does
docs.text:
Layer 2 is a multi-step pipeline that converts raw signals into intelligence. For each signal it validates intake, hydrates evidence, normalizes the signal, routes it for quality, builds atomic claims, fingerprints, and clusters related signals into events. For each cluster it then classifies the event, scores its significance deterministically, generates a GCP-grounded impact assessment, and upserts a DetectedChange. See Layer 2 — Intelligence Pipeline for the full 15 steps.

Note

Impact analysis is grounded in Godrej Consumer Products (GCP) as the home company. It reasons about affected GCP categories and markets and about competitors such as HUL, P&G India, ITC, Marico, Dabur, and Reckitt. See Scoring & Impact.

docs.title: 2. Run the pipeline
docs.text:
layer2-dev-run is the canonical local command for a Layer 2 run over pending signals.

ci-agent layer2-dev-run
# equivalent: python -m app.cli layer2-dev-run
# add --limit to cap how many signals are processed

The run prints counters: signals seen/processed/archived, clusters created/updated, detected changes created, alert candidates and digest entries created, LLM calls, and any failures.

docs.title: 3. Inspect the results
docs.text:
List the event clusters and the detected changes the run produced:

ci-agent list-event-clusters --limit 20
ci-agent list-detected-changes --limit 20

docs.title: 4. Read a DetectedChange
docs.text:
A DetectedChange is the central deliverable. Look for these fields:

  • headline / title — the one-line summary of the event.
  • so_what — why it matters to GCP.
  • recommended_action — the suggested response.
  • significance — the band the deterministic scorer assigned: High (≥75), Medium (≥40), Low (≥15), or Archive.
  • category — the classified event category.

Changes scored in the Archive band are stored with status archived; everything else is ready.

docs.title: 5. View it in the panel
docs.text: Open http://localhost:8000/admin/panel and go to the Changes screen under Intelligence. Click a change to drill into its impact assessment, evidence, and the feedback form. See Intelligence Screens.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Your First Feedback Loop — submit a verdict on one of these changes.
  • Layer 2 — Intelligence Pipeline — the pipeline concepts and diagrams.
  • Scoring & Impact — how significance and impact are computed.

docs.title: Tutorial — Your First Scan (Layer 1)
docs.text: In this tutorial you will run Layer 1 end-to-end on your machine and read the candidate signals it produces. Layer 1 is the ingestion stage: for each configured source it fetches content, persists raw and normalized data, diffs against the previous scan, and runs an analyzer that emits CandidateSignal rows — the input to Layer 2.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You completed Configuration & First Config Load — competitors and sources are loaded.
  • Your virtual environment is active.
  • You are running offline with the mock providers (the default), so no keys are needed.

docs.title: 1. What Layer 1 does
docs.text:
For each due Source, Layer 1 dispatches a source-type-specific adapter to fetch content, persists the results (RawArtifact, NormalizedDocument, DocumentBlock, SourceItem), then runs an analyzer that applies a cheap deterministic gate and — only when needed — an LLM call, producing LowLevelDelta → ChangePackage → CandidateSignal. For a deeper explanation, see Layer 1 — Source Scanning.

Note

The first scan of any source establishes a baseline — it records what exists but emits only a baseline_created delta and no candidate signals. Signals appear from the second scan onward, when there is a previous state to diff against. This is expected.

docs.title: 2. Run the scan
docs.text:
dev-run-once is the canonical local command for a full Layer 1 run. It scans all due sources and prints a summary table.

ci-agent dev-run-once
# equivalent: python -m app.cli dev-run-once

docs.title: 3. Read the summary table
docs.text: The command prints a per-source summary: which adapter and analyzer ran, how many artifacts, documents, and items were persisted, and how many candidate signals were produced. On the first run, expect signal counts of zero (baseline). Run it a second time to see change-driven signals appear.

docs.title: 4. Inspect the signals
docs.text:
List the candidate signals the scan produced:

ci-agent list-candidate-signals --limit 20
# add --verbose for more detail, or filter with --status / --type

Then drill into a single signal by ID:

ci-agent show-signal <signal-id>

Each signal carries a signal_type, a preliminary category, a title and summary, entities, evidence, a confidence score, and whether an LLM was used (llm_used).

docs.title: 5. What just happened
docs.text:
The scan worker ran this chain for each source:

  1. Adapter fetched the source and returned artifacts, normalized documents, and discovered items.
  2. The worker persisted raw artifacts to the blob store and normalized documents/items to the database.
  3. The analyzer loaded the previous state, computed deterministic deltas, and ran the cheap gate — which decides per change: suppress noise, promote as a candidate without an LLM, or send for llm_review.
  4. For llm_review changes, the analyzer called the LLM; otherwise it built the signal deterministically.
  5. Results were persisted as CandidateSignal rows with status candidate.

For the full 12-step worker flow and the adapter/analyzer patterns, see Layer 1 — Source Scanning.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• From Signals to a Scored Report (Layer 2) — turn these candidate signals into scored intelligence.
  • Layer 1 — Source Scanning — the concepts and diagrams behind this run.

docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text: This tutorial takes you from a clean clone to a running server with the admin panel open in your browser. Everything here works offline — no API keys required. When you finish, you will have a virtual environment, an initialized database, and a live FastAPI server at http://localhost:8000/admin/panel.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+ on your PATH (python --version).
  • git for cloning the repository.
  • The Azure DevOps repository URL for competitive-intel.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository and create a virtual environment
docs.text:
WindowsLinux / macOS 
git clone <azure-devops-url>
cd competitive-intel
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate

git clone <azure-devops-url>
cd competitive-intel
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: 2. Install the package (with dev extras)
docs.text:
Install the project in editable mode so your code changes take effect without reinstalling. The [dev] extra adds the test and lint tooling.

pip install -e ".[dev]"

This also registers the CLI entry point ci-agent, so ci-agent <cmd> is equivalent to python -m app.cli <cmd> everywhere in these docs.

Note

The test suite runs fully offline against the mock LLM provider with no keys configured. After installing, you can confirm the environment with pytest.

docs.title: 3. Create your .env from the template
docs.text:
Copy the safe template to a real .env. The template ships with offline-friendly defaults (mock providers), so you can leave it as-is for the tutorials.

cp .env.example .env

Warning

Never commit your .env. It is gitignored on purpose. .env.example is the safe, secret-free template — put only placeholders there, never real keys. See Configuration for the keys you will set later for a real-LLM run.

docs.title: 4. Initialize the database
docs.text:
Create the schema. Locally this is a SQLite file at data/ci_local.db.

ci-agent init-db
# equivalent: python -m app.cli init-db

This runs create_all plus a safe column-add pass. If you are working with Alembic migrations instead, use ci-agent init-db --alembic (see Backup & Migrations).

Warning

Never commit data/*.db or the local blob store — they hold real competitor data. Both are gitignored.

docs.title: 5. Start the server and open the panel
docs.text:
uvicorn app.main:app --reload

Then open the admin panel:

http://localhost:8000/admin/panel

The panel is a single static HTML file served by the app — there is no separate frontend build.

Note

Starting the server does not start a scan worker. In server mode the app only enqueues jobs; the tutorials execute scans directly via the CLI. See System Architecture for why.

docs.title: 6. Verify
docs.text:
Confirm the API is up with the health check:

curl http://localhost:8000/admin/health

You should get a healthy response, and the admin panel should load its dashboard without errors.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Configuration & First Config Load — set your environment and load competitors from YAML.

docs.title: Add a Competitor & Sources
docs.text: This guide walks you through registering a new competitor and its sources so the scanner can start collecting signals. You can do this in bulk from a YAML config file (best for initial setup) or one at a time through the API/admin panel (best for incremental changes). By the end you will have a Competitor row with one or more Source rows attached to it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The database has been initialized (ci-agent init-db). See Installation & Setup.
  • You know which source types you need (website_page, website_scope, news_search, careers, blog, social).
  • For API/panel edits, the server is running (uvicorn app.main:app --reload).

docs.title: Option A — Edit YAML and load it
docs.text: This is the fastest way to add several competitors and their sources at once. The loader (app/admin/yaml_loader.py) reads a YAML file and creates one Competitor per entry plus a Source per sources: item.

docs.title: Step 1 — Add the competitor block
docs.text:
Edit examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml (or a copy) and append a competitor. Identity fields map to the competitor's *_json columns and are used later for relevance and disambiguation.

competitors:
  - name: Marico Limited
    description: FMCG major, hair and edible oils
    market_positioning: Value + premium personal care
    tier: Tier1                      # Tier1 | Tier2 | Tier3
    aliases: [Marico, Marico Ltd]
    legal_names: [Marico Limited]
    known_domains: [marico.com]
    brand_names: [Parachute, Saffola, Livon]
    product_names: [hair oil, edible oil]
    leadership_names: [Saugata Gupta]
    industry_terms: [FMCG, personal care]
    negative_terms: [Marico County]  # disambiguation, filters false hits
    custom_keywords: [D2C, premiumisation]
    sources:
      - name: Marico website scope
        source_type: website_scope
        url: https://marico.com/
        frequency: weekly            # daily | weekly | manual
        config:                      # free-form; OVERRIDES matching .env keys
          seed_urls: [https://marico.com/newsroom]
          include_patterns: [/brands/, /news/]
          exclude_patterns: [/privacy, /cookie]
          max_pages_per_scan: 25
      - name: Marico news search
        source_type: news_search
        config: {provider: tavily, query_budget: 12, recency_window_days: 7}
      - name: Marico careers
        source_type: careers
        config: {ats_type: auto_detect}
      - name: Marico social
        source_type: social
        config: {linkedin_company_url: https://www.linkedin.com/company/marico, max_posts: 20}

Note

The per-source config: block overrides matching keys from .env. For example, setting provider: tavily on a news_search source wins over the global NEWS_PROVIDER setting.

docs.title: Step 2 — Load the config
docs.text:
ci-agent load-config examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml
# equivalent to: python -m app.cli load-config examples/config/godrej_competitors.yaml

The loader prints {competitors_created, sources_created} counts.

Warning

load-config always inserts — it does no dedup or upsert. Re-running it on the same file creates duplicate competitors and sources. To add just one competitor to an existing DB, load a file that contains only the new competitor, or use Option B.

docs.title: Option B — Add via the API or panel
docs.text: Use this for incremental, one-off additions where a full config reload would create duplicates.

docs.title: Step 1 — Create the competitor
docs.text:
POST /admin/competitors
{
  "name": "Marico Limited",
  "description": "FMCG major, hair and edible oils",
  "market_positioning": "Value + premium personal care",
  "tier": "Tier1",
  "aliases_json": ["Marico", "Marico Ltd"],
  "known_domains_json": ["marico.com"],
  "brand_names_json": ["Parachute", "Saffola"],
  "negative_terms_json": ["Marico County"],
  "is_active": true
}

Returns 201 with the created competitor (including its id).

docs.title: Step 2 — Add sources
docs.text:
Sources can be created nested under the competitor or flat (the flat form requires competitor_id).

POST /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/sources
{
  "source_type": "news_search",
  "name": "Marico news search",
  "config_json": {"provider": "tavily", "query_budget": 12, "recency_window_days": 7},
  "frequency": "weekly",
  "is_active": true
}

POST /admin/sources
{
  "competitor_id": "<competitor_id>",
  "source_type": "careers",
  "name": "Marico careers",
  "config_json": {"ats_type": "auto_detect"},
  "frequency": "weekly",
  "is_active": true
}

Both return 201. In the panel, the same forms live under Admin Control → Competitors and Admin Control → Sources.

docs.title: Choosing source types and config
docs.text:
source_type Typical config keys website_page (single URL, no extra config) website_scope seed_urls, include_patterns, exclude_patterns, max_pages_per_scan news_search provider (bing/brave/tavily/auto), query_budget, recency_window_days, bing_market careers ats_type (auto_detect/greenhouse/lever/workday), greenhouse_token, lever_company, workday_url blog (RSS/HTML index URL) social linkedin_company_url, twitter_handle, max_posts, apify_token

See Configure a News Profile for richer news relevance control beyond the basic news_search config.

docs.title: Avoid duplicates on reload
docs.text:
Because load-config never deduplicates, adopt one of these habits:

  • Keep the master YAML authoritative and only run load-config against a fresh database (after init-db).
  • For live databases, add competitors via Option B (API/panel).
  • Soft-delete stray duplicates with DELETE /admin/competitors/{id} (deactivates, returns 204).

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
ci-agent status        # shows competitor / source counts

Or check the panel: Admin Control → Competitors lists what was created, and drilling into a competitor shows its sources.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Configure a News Profile to tune news relevance for this competitor.
  • Run a Manual Scan to collect the first signals from your new sources.
  • API — Competitors, Sources, Runs & Audit for the full endpoint and schema reference.

docs.title: Add a New Source Type (Adapter + Analyzer)
docs.text: This guide shows you how to extend Layer 1 with a brand-new source type end to end: a fetch adapter, an analysis analyzer, and registration in both registries. Once done, any Source with your new source_type will scan and produce CandidateSignal rows like the built-in types. For the architecture behind adapters and analyzers, see Layer 1 — Source Scanning.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A local dev checkout with the app installed (pip install -e ".[dev]").
  • Familiarity with the adapter/analyzer contracts (app/adapters/base.py, app/analysis/contracts.py).
  • Config loaded so you have a competitor to attach a test source to.

Correct paths (doc-drift correction)

CLAUDE.md refers to app/analyzers/ and flat <type>_adapter.py files — that is outdated and wrong. The real layout is per-type packages:

  • Adapter: app/adapters/<type>/adapter.py
  • Analyzer: app/analysis/<type>/analyzer.py
  • Register in app/adapters/registry.py AND app/analysis/registry.py

docs.title: Step 1 — Write the adapter
docs.text:
Create app/adapters/<type>/adapter.py. The adapter fetches and normalizes; it does no LLM work. Implement the SourceAdapter protocol — a single scan() method returning an AdapterScanResult.

# app/adapters/<type>/adapter.py
import httpx
from app.core.config import get_settings
from app.schemas.adapter import (
    AdapterScanResult, FetchedSourceArtifact,
    AdapterNormalizedDocument, AdapterDiscoveredItem,
)

ADAPTER_NAME = "<type>"

class MyAdapter:
    def scan(self, source, competitor, context: dict) -> AdapterScanResult:
        settings = get_settings()
        cfg = source.config_json or {}
        # All adapter HTTP uses verify=False (deliberate — corporate proxy).
        resp = httpx.get(source.url, timeout=settings.HTTP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, verify=False)
        return AdapterScanResult(
            adapter_name=ADAPTER_NAME,
            source_type="<type>",
            fetched_artifacts=[FetchedSourceArtifact(...)],
            normalized_documents=[AdapterNormalizedDocument(...)],
            discovered_items=[AdapterDiscoveredItem(
                item_type="<some SourceItemType>",
                url="...",
                fingerprint="...",   # REQUIRED — stable dedup key per item
            )],
            warnings=[],
            metadata={},
        )

Info

verify=False on adapter HTTP is intentional (corporate proxy). Do not "fix" it. Reuse helpers in app/core/hashing.py and app/core/urls.py for content hashes and URL canonicalization.

Every AdapterDiscoveredItem must carry a fingerprint — it is the unique key for SourceItem (UNIQUE(source_id, fingerprint)) and drives appearance/disappearance detection.

docs.title: Step 2 — Write the analyzer
docs.text:
Create app/analysis/<type>/analyzer.py. Implement the SourceAnalyzer protocol's analyze() method returning a SourceAnalysisResult. The analyzer loads previous state, computes deterministic deltas, runs the cheap gate, and only calls the LLM when the gate says so.

# app/analysis/<type>/analyzer.py
from app.analysis.cheap_gate import evaluate_change_package
from app.schemas.analysis import SourceAnalysisResult

class MyAnalyzer:
    def analyze(self, source, competitor, scan_run, adapter_result,
                persisted_scan_objects, repositories, llm_provider) -> SourceAnalysisResult:
        # 1. Load previous state via repositories lambdas
        prev_items = repositories["list_previous_items_for_source"](source.id)

        # 2. First scan → emit only a baseline_created delta, NO signals
        # 3. Build LowLevelDeltaDraft + ChangePackage drafts deterministically

        # 4. Cheap gate decides per change package
        decision = evaluate_change_package(change_package)
        # -> no_action | suppress_noise | llm_review | candidate_without_llm

        # 5. Only on llm_review, call the LLM (structured JSON)
        if decision == "llm_review":
            result = llm_provider.complete_json(
                prompt_name="<type>_interpreter", prompt_version="v1",
                system_prompt="...", user_payload={...}, response_schema={...},
            )
            # record an LLMTraceDraft; build a CandidateSignalDraft

        return SourceAnalysisResult(
            low_level_deltas=[...], change_packages=[...],
            candidate_signals=[...], llm_traces=[...],
            warnings=[], metadata={},
        )

Notes:

  • repositories is a dict of accessor lambdas (list_previous_documents_for_source, list_previous_items_for_source, feedback_suppressions, db, …).
  • First scan of any source is baseline-only — emit a baseline_created delta and no candidate signals.
  • Put prompts in app/analysis/<type>/prompts.py. Adapters never call the LLM; analysis is the only LLM point in Layer 1.

docs.title: Step 3 — Register in BOTH registries
docs.text:
This is the step most commonly missed. The source type string must appear in both factories.

# app/adapters/registry.py  → build_default_adapter_registry()
registry["<type>"] = MyAdapter()

# app/analysis/registry.py  → build_default_analyzer_registry()
registry["<type>"] = MyAnalyzer()

If either registration is missing, the worker resolves no adapter/analyzer and fails the job (_fail_job → retry → dead-letter).

docs.title: Step 4 — Add enums if needed
docs.text:
If your adapter emits a new kind of item or artifact, add values to app/core/enums.py:

  • SourceType — add <type> so it validates on Source creation.
  • SourceItemType — if you discover a new item kind (e.g. podcast_episode).
  • ArtifactType — if you fetch a new raw format.

docs.title: Step 5 — Set metadata for telemetry
docs.text: The worker wraps your adapter and analyzer in observe_agent(...) with stage=source_type (adapter) and stage=f"{source_type}_analyze" (analyzer). Populate metadata on your results and call obs.set_output_count() where relevant so the observability screens show your new stage correctly.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Attach a test source with your new source_type to a competitor, then run a full local Layer 1 scan:

ci-agent dev-run-once
ci-agent list-candidate-signals --limit 20 --verbose

Remember: the first scan of a source emits only a baseline (no signals). Run it twice, changing the target between runs, to see deltas become candidate signals.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Layer 1 — Source Scanning for the adapter/analyzer/cheap-gate model and the worker flow.
  • Data Model & Enums for SourceItemType, ArtifactType, and related schemas.
  • Run a Manual Scan to exercise your new type through the console/API.

docs.title: Compile & Activate Policy Packs
docs.text: This guide shows you how to compile approved agent policy rules into a CompiledPolicyPack, read its health snapshot, simulate the combined runtime budget, and activate it within the token/rule budget gates. Consolidation for over-budget packs is covered at the end. For how packs fit runtime prompt assembly, see Feedback & Learning Governance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Approved AgentPolicyRule rows exist for the target agent (see Review & Approve Feedback Proposals).
  • The server running (for API/panel) or a checkout (for CLI).

Budgets

Packs are bounded by hard limits: per-pack 400 tokens, per-run 800 tokens (across up to 5 packs), and max 8 rules per pack. Tokens are estimated at 1.3 tokens per word. NEAR_BUDGET_THRESHOLD is 0.80.

docs.title: Step 1 — Compile a pack
docs.text:
compile_pack loads the agent's active policy rules by priority, takes the first min(MAX_POLICY_RULES_PER_PACK, MAX_RULES_PER_PACK) = 8, numbers them into compiled_text, estimates tokens, and supersedes any prior active pack with the same (agent_name, pack_name).

Via CLI:

ci-agent compile-policies <agent_name> [pack_name]

Via API — three modes:

POST /admin/feedback/policy-packs/compile
{
  "agent_name": "classifier",
  "pack_name": "default",
  "mode": "all-active"          // all-active | rule_ids | custom_text
}
  • all-active — compile all active rules for the agent.
  • rule_ids — compile a specific list of rule IDs.
  • custom_text — supply the compiled text directly.

The resulting pack is draft, or budget_exceeded if the estimate is over 400 tokens.

docs.title: Step 2 — Read the health snapshot
docs.text:
Compilation creates a PolicyPackHealthSnapshot and PolicyCoverageMap. Inspect them:

GET /admin/policy-health?agent_name=classifier      // pack + latest snapshot
GET /admin/policy-health/{id}                        // recomputes + persists a fresh snapshot
GET /admin/policy-health/{id}/coverage-map

The snapshot reports budget_utilization, health_status (healthy / near_budget_limit / budget_exceeded), duplicate detection (rules sharing the first-60-character prefix), and an issues_json list. The coverage map lists included rule IDs, superseded rule IDs, and covered active evaluation-case IDs.

docs.title: Step 3 — Simulate the combined budget
docs.text:
Before activating, check the total runtime cost across all active packs the agent would load at once.

POST /admin/policy-health/simulate

Returns a PolicyPackSimulationResult summing tokens across up to 5 active packs. activation_allowed is true only if the total is ≤ 800 (MAX_AGENT_POLICY_TOKENS_PER_RUN).

docs.title: Step 4 — Activate
docs.text:
POST /admin/feedback/policy-packs/{id}/activate

The activation gate raises a ValueError and blocks if the pack exceeds any limit:

  • token budget > 400, or
  • rule count > 8, or
  • duplicate rules present.

On success the pack becomes active with activated_at set and a fresh health snapshot.

Warning

Approving an agent_policy_rule proposal already auto-recompiles the agent's default pack. If you also compile manually, be aware you may supersede that auto-compiled pack — check GET /admin/policy-health afterward to confirm which pack is active.

docs.title: Step 5 — Consolidate an over-budget pack
docs.text:
If a pack is budget_exceeded or has duplicates, use LLM-assisted consolidation to merge/retire/convert rules.

POST /admin/policy-health/{id}/consolidate      // 201, LLM proposes consolidation
GET  /admin/policy-health/{id}/consolidation-proposals
PATCH /admin/policy-health/consolidation-proposals/{id}
{ "status": "applied" }                          // approved | rejected | applied

Applying a consolidation proposal recompiles the pack and retires the merged rules. Then re-run Step 3 and Step 4 to activate the slimmer pack.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Run the Evaluation Harness — activation may be gated on eval when REQUIRE_EVAL_BEFORE_POLICY_ACTIVATION is set.
  • Review & Approve Feedback Proposals for the rules that feed compilation.
  • Feedback & Learning Governance for the compilation flow and runtime gating.

docs.title: Configure a News Profile
docs.text: This guide shows you how to create and tune a competitor news profile — the rich configuration that drives query generation and relevance filtering for news_search sources. You will create a profile, preview the queries it generates, dry-run relevance against a sample article, and version/roll back changes safely. For how the news adapter and query planner use this profile, see Layer 1 — Source Scanning.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The competitor already exists (see Add a Competitor & Sources).
  • The server is running (uvicorn app.main:app --reload).
  • The competitor has (or will have) a news_search source.

docs.title: What a news profile controls
docs.text:
A CompetitorNewsProfile supplies the query planner (build_queries_from_profile) and the relevance gate (profile_relevance_check) with:

  • Identity & disambiguation: display_name, short_name, parent_company, legal_names_json, aliases_json (each alias can require context terms), negative_terms_json, exclusion_rules_json.
  • Brands: brands_json (each brand can require company context / required terms / active flag).
  • Markets: primary_market, monitored_markets_json, excluded_markets_json, global_parent_policy.
  • Sources of truth: official_domains_json, newsroom_urls_json, investor_urls_json, careers_urls_json.
  • Tuning: industry_terms_json, strategic_keywords_json, leaders_json, query_config_json, relevance_config_json, source_trust_json.

When an active profile exists, the news adapter picks it up via context["news_profile"] (or the DB) and uses build_queries_from_profile; otherwise it falls back to build_queries(competitor).

docs.title: Step 1 — Create the profile
docs.text:
POST /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/news-profile
{
  "display_name": "Hindustan Unilever",
  "short_name": "HUL",
  "parent_company": "Unilever",
  "tier": "Tier1",
  "aliases_json": [{"alias": "HUL", "requires_context": false}],
  "brands_json": [{"brand": "Dove", "requires_company_context": true, "active": true}],
  "primary_market": "India",
  "monitored_markets_json": ["India"],
  "official_domains_json": ["hul.co.in", "unilever.com"],
  "negative_terms_json": ["Hulu", "Hull City"],
  "query_config_json": {"query_budget": 12, "recency_window_days": 7},
  "relevance_config_json": {}
}

Returns 201 and records version v1 plus an audit entry. A 409 means a profile already exists for that competitor — use PATCH instead. In the panel, use Admin Control → News Profiles.

docs.title: Step 2 — Preview generated queries
docs.text:
Before scanning, check what the query planner will actually search for. This is a read-only dry run — no fetching happens.

GET /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/news-profile/preview-queries?budget=10

{
  "source": "...",
  "profile_version": 1,
  "queries": ["Hindustan Unilever news", "HUL Dove launch", "..."],
  "count": 10
}

If the queries look too broad or miss a brand, adjust aliases_json, brands_json, strategic_keywords_json, or query_config_json.query_budget and preview again.

docs.title: Step 3 — Test relevance
docs.text:
Dry-run the relevance gate against a sample article to confirm it passes real news and suppresses noise. When an active profile exists this runs profile_relevance_check; otherwise it uses fast_relevance_check.

POST /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/news-profile/test-relevance
{
  "title": "HUL launches new Dove serum in India",
  "snippet": "Hindustan Unilever announced ...",
  "url": "https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/..."
}

{
  "decision": "pass",          // pass | suppress | llm_review
  "reasons": ["alias match: HUL", "brand match: Dove", "market: India"]
}

Tune negative_terms_json and exclusion_rules_json to turn false hits into suppress, and adjust required-context terms if legitimate articles come back as suppress.

docs.title: Step 4 — Update and version
docs.text:
Every update snapshots the previous state into a CompetitorProfileVersion and writes an audit diff.

PATCH /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/news-profile
{
  "negative_terms_json": ["Hulu", "Hull City", "Unilever plc split"],
  "change_reason": "Filter parent-company restructuring noise"
}

List versions to review history:

GET /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/news-profile/versions?limit=20

docs.title: Step 5 — Roll back if needed
docs.text:
If a change made relevance worse, restore an earlier version. Rollback applies the chosen snapshot and records a new version marked is_rollback: true (it does not delete history).

POST /admin/competitors/{competitor_id}/news-profile/rollback/{version_id}

Re-run Step 2 and Step 3 after rolling back to confirm behavior is restored.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Admin Control Plane for the panel workflow (editor, versioning, preview, relevance test).
  • API — Schedules & News Profiles for the full endpoint and schema reference.
  • Run a Manual Scan to scan the news source with your new profile.

docs.title: Manage Suppressions
docs.text: This guide shows you how to create and remove suppressions so noisy URLs, domains, or repeat events stop generating signals and changes. The system has two independent suppression subsystems — a legacy one that acts in Layer 1 and a governance one that acts in Layer 2 — and you need to know which one you are touching. For the governance model overall, see Feedback & Learning Governance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The server running (for API/panel) or a checkout (for CLI).
  • A URL, domain, or event you want to stop seeing.

Two suppression systems — not unified

These two tables are separate and enforced at different points. Creating one does not affect the other.

Legacy (Layer 1) Governance (Layer 2) Model FeedbackSuppressionEntry SuppressionRule Code app/intelligence/feedback.py app/feedback/suppression.py Enforced at source_scan_worker.py + news analyzer (Layer 1) Layer 2 orchestrator Created via direct API/CLI proposal approval Supports title_pattern; domain is a note only source_url, domain, event_fingerprint

docs.title: Legacy suppression (Layer 1)
docs.text: Legacy entries stop candidate signals from being generated during scanning. They are checked in the scan worker and the news analyzer via get_active_suppressions / is_suppressed.

docs.title: Create a legacy suppression
docs.text:
POST /admin/feedback/suppressions
{
  "value": "https://example.com/press/holiday-notice",
  "reason": "Recurring low-value holiday post"
}

List and delete:

GET    /admin/feedback/suppressions?active_only=true&limit=50
DELETE /admin/feedback/suppressions/{id}

Via CLI:

ci-agent feedback-suppressions --limit 50

Legacy entries can match a title_pattern; domain-level suppression here is only recorded as a note, not enforced as a domain block.

docs.title: Governance suppression (Layer 2)
docs.text: Governance SuppressionRule rows gate the Layer 2 orchestrator: is_candidate_signal_suppressed (URL then domain) and is_event_suppressed (change:<id> fingerprints). They are not created directly — they come from approving a suppression proposal.

docs.title: Create a governance rule via proposal
docs.text:
1. Submit false_positive feedback on a DetectedChange. This generates a suppression_rule proposal (created on every false-positive occurrence — not frequency-gated). See Review & Approve Feedback Proposals.
  2. Approve the proposal. _activate_suppression creates one active SuppressionRule per all_values entry (deduping on already-active values).

Shortcut: if AUTO_CREATE_EXACT_URL_SUPPRESSION is enabled, a false_positive verdict also creates an exact-URL SuppressionRule immediately as a structural action (in addition to the proposal). AUTO_ARCHIVE_FALSE_POSITIVE similarly archives the change immediately.

List active rules:

GET /admin/feedback/suppression-rules

docs.title: Suppression types & TTLs
docs.text:
Governance rules come in three types, with default expiry governed by config flags:

Type Matches Default TTL flag Default source_url exact URL DEFAULT_SUPPRESSION_EXACT_URL_TTL_DAYS None (never expires) domain whole domain DEFAULT_SUPPRESSION_DOMAIN_TTL_DAYS None (never expires) event_fingerprint a specific event (change:<id>) DEFAULT_SUPPRESSION_EVENT_FINGERPRINT_TTL_DAYS 90

Rules respect expires_at; expired rules stop matching. Domain suppressions require human approval (REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL_FOR_DOMAIN_SUPPRESSION=True).

docs.title: Where each is enforced
docs.text:
• Legacy FeedbackSuppressionEntry — Layer 1, during scanning (worker + news analyzer). Stops candidate signals at the source.
  • Governance SuppressionRule — Layer 2, inside the orchestrator. Stops candidate signals from being promoted and suppresses already-detected events.

To fully silence a noisy source across both layers, add a legacy entry and a governance rule.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Review & Approve Feedback Proposals to approve the suppression-rule proposals that create governance rules.
  • Feedback & Learning Governance for how suppressions fit the wider governance lifecycle.

docs.title: Recover a Failed Run
docs.text: This guide shows you how to diagnose a scan that failed or got stuck, understand why, and re-drive it — by retrying failed sources, cleaning up stuck runs, or re-baselining a source. For the underlying error and retry semantics, see Error Handling, Retries & Status Codes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A ScanRun that failed or has failed jobs.
  • The server running (for API/panel) or a checkout (for CLI).

docs.title: Step 1 — Find the failure
docs.text:
Start at the run's jobs. Each SourceScanLog row carries the diagnostic fields.

GET /admin/runs/{scan_run_id}/jobs

Each job returns source_name, source_type, competitor_name, status (pending/running/success/failed/skipped), adapter_name, attempt_count, error_type, error_message, and candidate_signals_count. Look for status: failed and read error_type / error_message.

In the panel: Admin Control → Runs, then drill into the run to see the per-job table. Common error_type values come from the worker (adapter/analyzer exceptions, NotFound for missing source/competitor).

Note

A job stuck at running with no update is usually an interrupted run (the process died mid-scan), not an active one. Startup marks orphaned running PipelineRun/ScanRun/AgentRunTelemetry rows as interrupted, but a run left over from a crash before restart may still show running — treat it as stuck (see Step 4).

docs.title: Step 2 — Understand the retry model
docs.text:
The worker's retry behavior is asymmetric, which affects what "retry" means:

  • Pre-flight failures (e.g. adapter/analyzer not resolvable for the source type) call _fail_job, which marks the log failed and calls queue.retry. The queue increments the attempt count and dead-letters after MAX_QUEUE_ATTEMPTS (default 3).
  • Runtime failures (adapter or analyzer raises during scan/analyze) mark the job failed and ack the message — they are not retried automatically.
  • LLM failures never crash the job — the provider returns an LLMResult with error_message and empty output_json; the pipeline continues.

Warning

Because runtime adapter/analyzer failures ack (no auto-retry), a genuinely failed source scan will not re-run on its own. You must re-drive it explicitly with retry_failed (Step 3).

docs.title: Step 3 — Retry failed sources
docs.text:
Re-enqueue only the failed SourceScanLog rows for a run:

POST /admin/scan-requests
{
  "request_type": "retry_failed",
  "params_json": {"scan_run_id": "<failed_scan_run_id>"},
  "requested_by": "admin"
}

Returns 202. Remember a worker must consume the re-enqueued jobs — run ci-agent worker-once locally, or rely on the prod consumer. See Run a Manual Scan.

docs.title: Step 4 — Clean up stuck runs
docs.text:
If a run is wedged at running (crash, killed process), reset it so it no longer blocks visibility:

POST /admin/scan-runs/cleanup

This transitions running scan runs to abandoned. Restarting the server also marks orphaned running PipelineRun/ScanRun/AgentRunTelemetry rows as interrupted during startup.

docs.title: Step 5 — Re-baseline if needed
docs.text:
If a source's stored state is corrupt or you changed its config such that diffs are meaningless, re-baseline it. This clears last_scan_at, so the next scan is treated as a first scan (baseline only, no signals) and subsequent scans diff against the clean baseline.

POST /admin/scan-requests
{
  "request_type": "rebaseline",
  "params_json": {"source_id": "<source_id>"},
  "requested_by": "admin"
}

Note

The scan immediately after a rebaseline emits only a baseline and produces no candidate signals — that is expected. Run the source again to start seeing deltas.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Error Handling, Retries & Status Codes for _fail_job, dead-letter behavior, and status codes.
  • Troubleshooting for jobs-not-running, no-signals, and LLM error diagnoses.
  • Run a Manual Scan to re-run sources after recovery.

docs.title: Review & Approve Feedback Proposals
docs.text: This guide shows you how to work the human-review queue: list pending proposals mined from analyst feedback, understand their types and risk, and approve or reject them to activate policy. Approving a proposal is the gate that turns learned patterns into live suppression rules, weight profiles, or agent policy rules. For the full governance lifecycle, see Feedback & Learning Governance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Analyst feedback has been submitted on DetectedChange rows, producing proposals. See the first feedback loop tutorial.
  • The server running (for API/panel).

Governance never auto-approves

The governance pipeline is deterministic and never activates policy on its own. Every proposal sits at pending_human_review until a human approves it. (The legacy path may apply some effects immediately — that is separate; see Manage Suppressions.)

docs.title: Step 1 — List pending proposals
docs.text:
GET /admin/feedback/proposals?status=pending_human_review&limit=50

Returns the newest 50 proposals. In the panel, use Governance → Governance (the screen shows a red badge with the pending count and approve/reject controls).

docs.title: Step 2 — Understand proposal types and risk
docs.text:
Proposals are generated deterministically from mined patterns (_PROPOSAL_THRESHOLD=2). There are three builders:

Proposal type Generated when Risk suppression_rule verdict false_positive — every occurrence (not frequency-gated) low (≤2), else medium scoring_weight_change over_scored/under_scored, frequency ≥ 2, category present (±10%) high agent_policy_rule misclassified, wrong_geography, weak_evidence_overpromoted, false_positive, over_scored, under_scored, frequency ≥ 2 medium

Dual proposals

An over_scored/under_scored pattern at frequency ≥ 2 produces both a scoring_weight_change and an agent_policy_rule proposal (both targeting the scorer). Expect to review two related proposals, and decide on each independently.

The agent_policy_rule builder retargets by error type (e.g. misclassified → classifier, over_scored/under_scored → scorer), ignoring the feedback's own agent_name.

docs.title: Step 3 — Approve or reject
docs.text:
Only pending_human_review proposals can be approved.

POST /admin/feedback/proposals/{id}/approve
{
  "reviewer": "krishna",
  "edited_change_json": null
}
  • Approving as-is sets status approved. Supplying edited_change_json sets status edited_and_approved and activates the edited version.
  • Reject instead:
POST /admin/feedback/proposals/{id}/reject
{
  "reviewer": "krishna",
  "review_notes": "Legitimate event, not noise"
}

Warning

Approval always activates, regardless of the proposal's risk_level. There is no separate "approve but hold" — approving a high-risk weight change activates it immediately. (REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL_FOR_PROMPT_CHANGES only gates auto-activation, not this manual approval.)

docs.title: Step 4 — What activation does per type
docs.text:
_activate_proposal dispatches by proposal_type:

  • suppression_rule → _activate_suppression: creates one active SuppressionRule per all_values entry (dedupes on already-active values).
  • scoring_weight_change → _activate_weight_change: deep-copies the active weight profile, applies the new category_scores[cat], deactivates the old profile, inserts a new active ScoringWeightProfile (feedback_adjusted_<cat>).
  • agent_policy_rule → _activate_policy_rule: creates an active AgentPolicyRule and auto-recompiles that agent's default policy pack via PolicyCompiler().compile_pack().

docs.title: Step 5 — Verify runtime state
docs.text:
Confirm the change is live:

GET /admin/feedback/runtime-state

This shows the currently active rules, packs, weights, and suppressions. In the panel, Governance → Runtime State renders the same live view.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Compile & Activate Policy Packs to manage the packs that agent-policy-rule approvals recompile.
  • Manage Suppressions for the two suppression systems.
  • Feedback & Learning Governance for the proposal state machine and pattern mining.

docs.title: Run the Evaluation Harness
docs.text: This guide shows you how to create and approve evaluation cases, run a regression eval against a policy pack, read the tolerance-based results, and use eval as a gate before activating policy. The harness protects you from policy changes that quietly regress agent behavior. For where eval sits in governance, see Feedback & Learning Governance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The server running (for API/panel).
  • A policy pack to evaluate (see Compile & Activate Policy Packs).
  • For LLM-agent eval, a real LLM provider configured (otherwise the mock provider is used).

docs.title: Step 1 — Create and approve eval cases
docs.text:
Eval cases are API-created — no governance code auto-generates them. Create a case with the agent, its input, and the expected output.

POST /admin/feedback/eval-cases
{
  "agent_name": "final_classifier",
  "input_json": { "cluster": { "...": "..." } },
  "expected_output_json": { "final_category": "Product Launch" }
}

Returns 201; the case starts as draft. Approve it to make it active (only active cases run):

POST /admin/feedback/eval-cases/{id}/approve

List cases:

GET /admin/feedback/eval-cases?agent_name=final_classifier

docs.title: Step 2 — Run the eval
docs.text:
POST /admin/feedback/eval-runs
{
  "agent_name": "final_classifier",
  "policy_pack_id": "<pack_id>"
}

run_eval runs all active cases for the agent and writes an EvaluationRun (total / passed / failed + results_json). How each case runs depends on the agent:

  • scoring agent — deterministic: _run_scoring_agent builds a mock cluster/competitor/bundles and calls score_cluster (no LLM).
  • LLM agents — classification (final_classifier v1), impact_analysis (v2), news_relevance (v1) call complete_json with the real system prompt plus get_prompt_addendum.
  • Other agents — skipped.

docs.title: Step 3 — Read the results
docs.text:
Each case is graded by _compare with type-specific tolerances:

Expected type Pass condition bool exact match float within ±0.2 int within ±10% (minimum 1) list expected is a subset str case-insensitive match empty expected skipped

Inspect the EvaluationRun results_json for per-case pass/fail and the compared values. Failures point at cases where the current policy pack changed the agent's output beyond tolerance.

docs.title: Step 4 — Gate policy activation on eval
docs.text:
When REQUIRE_EVAL_BEFORE_POLICY_ACTIVATION=True, a policy pack should pass its eval before you activate it. The workflow is:

  1. Compile the pack (draft).
  2. Run the eval against that policy_pack_id (Step 2).
  3. Confirm failed == 0 (or acceptable), then activate the pack — see Compile & Activate Policy Packs.

Note

The eval harness exercises agent behavior only; it does not itself flip a pack to active. Use the eval result to decide whether to call the activate endpoint.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Compile & Activate Policy Packs to activate a pack once it passes eval.
  • Feedback & Learning Governance for the eval harness in the wider lifecycle.

docs.title: Run a Manual Scan
docs.text: This guide shows you how to trigger scans on demand — from the admin panel, the API, or the CLI — using each of the six request types. Manual scans are how you collect signals outside the schedule, re-run failures, or drive Layer 2 on its own. For the console UI in depth, see Manual Run Console.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Competitors and sources are configured (see Add a Competitor & Sources).
  • The server is running for panel/API options; a checkout with the CLI for CLI options.

The server only enqueues

In server mode, POST /admin/scan-requests and the panel console enqueue jobs onto the queue — nothing consumes them automatically. A worker must run for jobs to execute: the CLI commands (worker-once, dev-run-once, run-pipeline) or, in production, a separate Service Bus consumer. The exception is layer2_only, which runs the orchestrator directly and skips the queue.

docs.title: The six request types
docs.text: request_type What it does params_json all_sources Enqueue every due source (schedule_scan with no selection) {} competitor_sources Enqueue all active sources for one competitor {"competitor_id": "..."} single_source Enqueue one specific source {"source_id": "..."} layer2_only Run the Layer 2 orchestrator on existing signals (no queue) {"scan_run_id": "...", "competitor_id": "...", "limit": 20} (all optional) retry_failed Re-enqueue failed SourceScanLog rows from a run {"scan_run_id": "..."} rebaseline Clear last_scan_at, then enqueue the source (next scan re-baselines) {"source_id": "..."}

docs.title: Option A — From the panel
docs.text:
1. Open Admin Control → Scan Console in the panel (/admin/panel).
  2. Select a request type. The form shows/hides the competitor picker (competitor_sources) and source-ID field (single_source, rebaseline) accordingly.
  3. Submit. The panel POSTs to /admin/scan-requests and receives a 202.
  4. Watch the Live Run / Scan Runs widgets, which poll /admin/runs/current and /admin/runs/{id}/jobs.

docs.title: Option B — From the API
docs.text:
POST /admin/scan-requests
{
  "request_type": "competitor_sources",
  "params_json": {"competitor_id": "<competitor_id>"},
  "requested_by": "admin"
}

Returns 202 with a ScanRequestOut (status starts pending/created, then transitions running → completed/failed). The request is handled in the background by _run_scan_in_background.

Watch progress:

GET /admin/scan-requests?limit=20          // request status
GET /admin/runs/current                    // latest running/most-recent run
GET /admin/runs/{scan_run_id}/jobs         // per-source job status

docs.title: Option C — From the CLI
docs.text:
The CLI both enqueues and runs a worker, so jobs actually execute locally.

# Enqueue due sources, then drain the queue once:
ci-agent schedule-once
ci-agent worker-once

# One-shot full local Layer 1 run + summary table (canonical for dev):
ci-agent dev-run-once

# Layer 1 then Layer 2 in sequence:
ci-agent run-pipeline --limit 100

# Layer 2 only, over existing candidate signals:
ci-agent process-layer2 --limit 100
# or scoped:
ci-agent process-layer2 --scan-run-id <id>

ci-agent <cmd> is equivalent to python -m app.cli <cmd>.

docs.title: layer2_only vs the queue types
docs.text: layer2_only is special: it invokes CoreIntelligenceOrchestrator directly and never touches the queue, so it runs to completion even in server mode with no worker. All the other request types enqueue Layer 1 jobs and therefore need a worker/consumer running (see the note above). The API equivalent of layer2_only is also exposed as POST /admin/run-layer2 {"limit": 20, "competitor_id": "..."}.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Manual Run Console for the console's param builders and run lifecycle.
  • Recover a Failed Run when jobs fail — including retry_failed and cleanup.
  • API — Competitors, Sources, Runs & Audit for scan-request and run-visibility endpoints.

docs.title: Assemble & Send a Weekly Digest
docs.text: This guide shows you how to build the weekly intelligence digest from ready DetectedChange rows, preview it, send it to recipients, and check delivery logs. It also covers the immediate high-significance alerts and Teams cards that run alongside the digest. For where delivery sits in the pipeline, see Layer 2 — Intelligence Pipeline.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• DetectedChange rows with status ready from the last 7 days (produced by Layer 2).
  • SMTP configured to actually send email (see the note below).
  • The server running (for API/panel) or a checkout (for CLI).

Email is skipped without SMTP

If SMTP_HOST is unset, email delivery is skipped (logged as skipped) — assembly and preview still work, but nothing is sent. Configure SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT (465 for SSL, else STARTTLS), SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASSWORD, SMTP_FROM_EMAIL, and DEFAULT_RECIPIENTS. The email SSL context is permissive by design (corporate proxy) — do not "fix" it. Use placeholders for any secrets, never real credentials.

docs.title: Step 1 — Assemble the digest
docs.text:
DigestAssembler.assemble_weekly pulls DetectedChange rows with status ready from the last 7 days, groups them by competitor, sorts by significance, and persists a WeeklyDigest in draft status with branded HTML and a plain-text version.

Via CLI:

ci-agent digest-assemble            # optional: --week YYYY-Www
ci-agent digest-list --limit 20

Via API:

POST /admin/weekly-digests/assemble        // 201, creates a draft
GET  /admin/weekly-digests?limit=20

The week label is ISO format (YYYY-Www).

docs.title: Step 2 — Preview
docs.text:
Review the rendered digest before sending.

ci-agent digest-preview --digest-id <id>          # HTML
ci-agent digest-preview --digest-id <id> --plain  # plain text

Via API:

GET /admin/weekly-digests/{id}/html

In the panel, Delivery → Digests offers assemble / preview / send for each WeeklyDigest.

docs.title: Step 3 — Send
docs.text:
ci-agent digest-send --digest-id <id> --to analyst@example.com

Via API:

POST /admin/weekly-digests/{id}/send
{ "recipients": ["analyst@example.com"] }

On success, the WeeklyDigest transitions to sent (with sent_at and recipients_json) and a DeliveryLog row is written. If SMTP_HOST is unset, the send is recorded as skipped.

To assemble and send in one step:

POST /admin/weekly-digests/assemble-and-send

docs.title: Step 4 — Teams alerts & immediate high-significance alerts
docs.text:
Digest email is not the only delivery channel:

  • High-significance immediate alerts: during Layer 2 (step 12), when a DetectedChange lands in the High band, EmailDelivery.send_high_significance_alert fires immediately — independent of the weekly digest.
  • Teams cards: TeamsDelivery.send_card / send_alert post a MessageCard to TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL (color by significance, verify=False, 10s timeout). If TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL is unset, Teams delivery is skipped. Each attempt writes a DeliveryLog (channel teams_webhook).

docs.title: Step 5 — Check delivery logs
docs.text:
Confirm what actually went out (or was skipped):

GET /admin/delivery-logs?limit=50

In the panel, Delivery → Delivery Logs shows the same. Look for sent vs skipped and any error detail.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Intelligence Screens for the panel's digest and delivery-log views.
  • Deployment for the WeeklyDigestScheduler (Mondays 08:00) and SMTP/Teams configuration in production.

docs.title: Tune Scoring Weights
docs.text: This guide shows you how to view and adjust the significance-scoring weights that decide whether a change lands in the High / Medium / Low / Archive band. You will inspect the active weight profile, adjust a category weight, activate a new profile, and understand how analyst feedback can move weights automatically. For the scoring model itself, see Scoring & Impact.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The server running (for API/panel) or a checkout (for CLI).
  • Some scored DetectedChange rows to observe the effect (optional but recommended).

docs.title: How weights work
docs.text: Scoring (score_cluster) is fully deterministic. The orchestrator loads exactly one active ScoringWeightProfile per run via load_active_weights, which merges that profile's weights_json over DEFAULT_WEIGHTS. There is always exactly one profile with is_active=True.

docs.title: Step 1 — View the active weights
docs.text:
GET /admin/scoring-weights
GET /admin/scoring-weights/defaults

Or via CLI:

ci-agent scoring-weights-list
ci-agent scoring-weights-show

The profile's weights_json contains the tunable groups — notably category_scores (per-category points such as Product Launch / Pricing) alongside the tier, authority, corroboration, novelty, and confidence components.

docs.title: Step 2 — Adjust a weight
docs.text:
The safest incremental change is to nudge a single key on an existing profile.

ci-agent scoring-weights-adjust --profile-id <id> --key category_scores.Pricing --delta 3 --reason "Pricing moves under-scored"

Via API, patch a profile (merges the supplied updates):

PATCH /admin/scoring-weights/{id}
{
  "weight_updates": {"category_scores": {"Pricing": 21}}
}

docs.title: Step 3 — Create and activate a profile
docs.text:
To make larger changes without mutating the current profile, create a new one and activate it. Creating does not auto-activate.

ci-agent scoring-weights-create --name "pricing-emphasis" --no-activate
ci-agent scoring-weights-activate <new_profile_id>

Via API:

POST /admin/scoring-weights            // 201, does NOT auto-activate
PUT  /admin/scoring-weights/{id}/activate

Activating a profile deactivates whichever profile was previously active — only one is ever active.

docs.title: Step 4 — Understand feedback-driven auto-adjustment
docs.text:
Weights can also change through the feedback system, via two distinct paths:

  • Governance path (deterministic ±10%): an over_rated/under_rated verdict, once its pattern reaches frequency ≥ 2, produces a scoring_weight_change proposal. On approval, _activate_weight_change deep-copies the active profile, sets category_scores[cat] to the proposed value (decrease max(1, round(cur*0.9)), increase round(cur*1.1)), deactivates the old profile, and inserts a new active one named feedback_adjusted_<cat>.
  • Legacy path (LLM): submitting over_rated, under_rated, false_positive, or missed feedback triggers decide_weight_adjustments_with_llm + apply_llm_weight_adjustments, appending deltas (clamped [-30, 30]) to adjustment_log_json.

Note

The governance path never auto-applies — the weight change only takes effect after a human approves the proposal. See Review & Approve Feedback Proposals.

docs.title: Step 5 — Verify the effect
docs.text:
Re-run Layer 2 over a set of signals and inspect the resulting bands:

ci-agent process-layer2 --limit 50
ci-agent list-detected-changes --limit 50

Check that changes in the tuned category now fall into the intended band (High ≥ 75, Medium ≥ 40, Low ≥ 15, else Archive). Each change stores its full score_breakdown_json so you can confirm the component contributions.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Scoring & Impact for the full component/band model and reliability multiplier.
  • Review & Approve Feedback Proposals to approve feedback-driven weight changes.
  • API — Intelligence & Delivery for the scoring-weights endpoints.

docs.title: Backup & Migrations
docs.text: This page covers the database's storage model, the current (partially adopted) migration strategy, how to create and apply schema changes, and how to back up and restore the database and blob artifacts. Read Deployment first if you have not chosen an environment yet.

docs.title: The database
docs.text:
• Local: SQLite at data/ci_local.db (DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///./data/ci_local.db). The engine (app/db/session.py) opens SQLite with check_same_thread=False, timeout=120, and a connect-time PRAGMA setting journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=NORMAL, busy_timeout=120000. WAL mode means the on-disk database is accompanied by -wal and -shm sidecar files — include those when copying a live database.
  • In-memory: sqlite:///:memory: uses a StaticPool (critical for tests to share one connection).
  • Production: Azure SQL, via a SQLAlchemy-compatible DATABASE_URL. Models are portable SQLAlchemy 2.0; the WAL/StaticPool specifics are SQLite-only.

Warning

Never commit data/*.db. The local database contains real competitor data and is gitignored. The same applies to blob artifacts under LOCAL_BLOB_ROOT — treat them as sensitive.

docs.title: Migrations: the reality
docs.text:
Schema management is partially migrated to Alembic. In practice the schema is created and evolved two ways:

  1. Base.metadata.create_all() — run by both ci-agent init-db and at server startup. This creates any missing tables from app/db/models.py.
  2. _safe_add_columns — idempotent column additions applied in code for incremental fields.

Alembic (alembic.ini, alembic/) is present and wired (target_metadata = Base.metadata, NullPool), but the revision chain is minimal:

  • ec80a363b261_initial_schema — down_revision = None, an empty placeholder stub.
  • b3f2a8c94d12_admin_control_plane — the current head. Hand-written and idempotent (guarded by table_exists / index_exists / column_exists). Adds source_schedules, scan_requests, competitor_news_profiles, competitor_profile_versions, admin_audit_logs, and the source_scan_logs.news_profile_version_id column.

Note

Because most tables are born from create_all(), an autogenerated Alembic migration on a fresh checkout may see the schema as already up to date. Alembic is the intended long-term path but is not yet the source of truth. See Release Notes for this drift item.

docs.title: Create and apply migrations
docs.text:
To add a schema change through Alembic:

# 1. Edit models in app/db/models.py, then autogenerate a revision
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add my_new_table"

# 2. Review the generated script under alembic/versions/ before applying

# 3. Apply to head
alembic upgrade head

You can also apply migrations through the CLI, which combines table creation with the Alembic upgrade:

ci-agent init-db --alembic     # create_all + _safe_add_columns, then alembic upgrade head

Plain ci-agent init-db (no flag) runs create_all + _safe_add_columns only, which is sufficient for local development and for standing up a fresh database.

Tip

If you hit "no such column" or similar schema errors after pulling changes, run ci-agent init-db (or alembic upgrade head) to bring the local schema forward. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Backing up blobs
docs.text:
Raw and normalized artifacts (fetched HTML, JSON, cleaned text) are stored in the blob store, not the database — the DB holds only URIs.

  • Local: artifacts live under LOCAL_BLOB_ROOT (default ./data/blob), referenced as local://<path>. Back up by copying that directory alongside the database.
  • Azure Blob: artifacts live in the AZURE_BLOB_CONTAINER (default ci-artifacts), referenced as azblob://<container>/<path>. Use standard Azure Blob backup / lifecycle / geo-replication policies.

A consistent backup is database + blob store together — the URIs in the DB must resolve to objects that still exist in the blob store.

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
To restore a local environment:

  1. Stop the server and any worker processes (so nothing holds the SQLite lock).
  2. Restore data/ci_local.db plus its -wal and -shm sidecar files (or checkpoint the WAL before backing up so the main file is complete).
  3. Restore the LOCAL_BLOB_ROOT directory so artifact URIs resolve.
  4. Restart and confirm health with ci-agent status and the Monitoring screens.

For Azure, restore the Azure SQL database from its point-in-time backup and ensure the blob container is at a matching point in time so azblob:// URIs remain valid.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Deployment — environment selection and startup behavior (including create_all at boot).
  • Data Model & Enums — the tables and columns you are migrating.
  • Troubleshooting — resolving schema errors.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
This page covers how to run the Competitive Intelligence Aggregator in production: switching from the local development stack to Azure-backed infrastructure, running the scan worker as a separate process, scheduling automated scans, understanding what happens at server startup, and publishing this documentation site.

For the exhaustive list of environment keys referenced here, see the Configuration & Environment reference.

docs.title: Environments: local vs production
docs.text:
The application selects its infrastructure at runtime through app/infra.py, driven by the ENVIRONMENT setting and the presence of Azure connection strings. There is no separate "prod build" — the same code runs both places and swaps implementations based on configuration.

Concern Local (ENVIRONMENT=local) Production (ENVIRONMENT=production) Queue InMemorySourceScanQueue AzureServiceBusSourceScanQueue Blob store LocalBlobStore (under LOCAL_BLOB_ROOT) AzureBlobStore LLM provider MockLLMProvider (or Azure OpenAI if keyed) AzureOpenAIProvider Database SQLite (data/ci_local.db, WAL mode) Azure SQL (SQLAlchemy-compatible) Config source .env file Azure Key Vault → environment

The selection logic is deliberately conservative: build_blob_store() and build_queue() return the Azure implementation only when ENVIRONMENT is not local AND the relevant connection string is set. If either condition is missing, they fall back to the local implementation. This means setting ENVIRONMENT=production alone is not enough — you must also provide the connection strings.

# Production environment (values are placeholders — never commit real secrets)
ENVIRONMENT=production
DATABASE_URL=mssql+pyodbc://<user>:<pw>@<server>.database.windows.net/<db>?driver=ODBC+Driver+18+for+SQL+Server

LLM_PROVIDER=azure_openai
AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT=https://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com
AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY=<key>
AZURE_OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4o

AZURE_SERVICE_BUS_CONNECTION_STRING=<connection-string>
AZURE_SERVICE_BUS_QUEUE_NAME=source-scan-jobs

AZURE_BLOB_CONNECTION_STRING=<connection-string>
AZURE_BLOB_CONTAINER=ci-artifacts

Danger

Never print, log, or commit real secrets. Use placeholders like <key> and https://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com in any file that lands in the repo. .env is gitignored; .env.example is the safe template. In production, prefer Azure Key Vault over a .env file.

docs.title: Azure-ready swaps
docs.text:
Each infrastructure dependency is behind a small interface so the local and Azure implementations are interchangeable. To move to Azure, set the environment (above) — no code change is required.

  • Queue → Azure Service Bus. AzureServiceBusSourceScanQueue (app/queue/azure_service_bus.py) serializes jobs as JSON bodies and uses lock-token ack / abandon / dead_letter semantics. Queue name defaults to source-scan-jobs.
  • Blob → Azure Blob. AzureBlobStore (app/storage/azure_blob.py) stores artifacts as azblob://<container>/<path>; the local store uses local://<path>. Container defaults to ci-artifacts.
  • LLM → Azure OpenAI. AzureOpenAIProvider (app/llm/azure_openai_provider.py) lazily constructs an openai.AzureOpenAI client (api-version 2024-08-01-preview), calls the deployment named by AZURE_OPENAI_MODEL, and writes an LLMCostLedger row per call. See LLM Abstraction.
  • Database → Azure SQL. Point DATABASE_URL at Azure SQL. Models are SQLAlchemy 2.0 and portable; note the SQLite-specific WAL/StaticPool behavior only applies to the local file/in-memory DB.

docs.title: The worker in production
docs.text:
Warning

In server mode, nothing consumes the queue automatically. The FastAPI server (and admin scan-requests) only enqueue jobs. The server-side scheduler (app/scheduler/__init__.py) starts a WeeklyDigestScheduler only — it does not periodically run source scans or drain the queue. You must run a worker/consumer separately, or jobs will sit unprocessed.

In production the pattern is a separate process consuming the Azure Service Bus queue and running SourceScanWorker.process_job for each message. Locally, the equivalent is CLI-driven execution:

# Local: enqueue due sources, then drain the queue in one process
ci-agent schedule-once    # enqueue only
ci-agent worker-once      # process queue only

# Or the all-in-one local run
ci-agent dev-run-once     # schedule + fetch + analyze

ci-agent <cmd> is equivalent to python -m app.cli <cmd>. See the CLI Reference and Run a Manual Scan.

docs.title: Scheduled scans
docs.text:
Two independent schedulers exist:

  • Layer 1 source scans are driven by SourceSchedule rows (one per source) and get_due_sources(). On the server these only advance schedules and enqueue — they still require a worker to execute. For unattended runs on Windows, run_daily_scan.bat is provided at the repo root and is ready to register with Windows Task Scheduler for a daily full scan.
:: run_daily_scan.bat — register with Windows Task Scheduler for a daily scan
  • Weekly digest is handled by the in-server WeeklyDigestScheduler, which fires Mondays at 08:00 (Asia/Kolkata) to assemble and send the weekly digest via Layer 3 delivery. See Assemble & Send a Weekly Digest.

Note

The WeeklyDigestScheduler is the only thing the server-side scheduler starts. It does not run scans. Treat source-scan scheduling (Task Scheduler / a Service Bus consumer) as a separate deployment concern.

docs.title: Startup behavior
docs.text:
When the FastAPI app boots (app/main.py), the startup hook performs several one-time actions:

  1. Base.metadata.create_all() — creates any missing tables (schema is primarily managed this way plus _safe_add_columns, not Alembic; see Backup & Migrations).
  2. Starts the scheduler — the WeeklyDigestScheduler described above.
  3. Seeds the price catalog — _seed_price_catalog() inserts an active LLMPriceCatalog row (USD/1k: input 0.005, output 0.015, cached 0.0025) so cost tracking works immediately.
  4. Wires the DB session factory into the LLM provider so per-call LLMCostLedger rows can be written.
  5. Orphan cleanup — marks any PipelineRun / ScanRun / AgentRunTelemetry rows still in running state (left over from a crash or restart) as interrupted.

Warning

Startup uses the deprecated FastAPI on_event hook rather than the newer lifespan handler. This is a known drift item (see Release Notes); it works but should be migrated.

docs.title: Publishing these docs
docs.text:
This documentation site is built with MkDocs Material and published as a static site through Azure DevOps.

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs build            # renders docs/ into static site/
# publish the site/ directory via the Azure DevOps pipeline

mkdocs build produces a self-contained site/ directory. Point the Azure DevOps release/pipeline at that folder to publish. Use mkdocs serve locally for a live preview while editing.
